chapter.name: Current Electricity
chapter.blurb: Charges in steady motion make an electric current, and this chapter follows that current from its definition through Ohm's law, resistivity and the drift of electrons that explains it, to the way resistivity changes with temperature and the heat a current produces. It then turns to cells, their emf and internal resistance and their series and parallel combinations, and ends with Kirchhoff's rules for analysing any network and the Wheatstone bridge as their application.

scope_in.item: Define steady current as net charge crossing an area per unit time (I = q/t, q = q+ - q-), interpret a negative value, and state the general definition as the limit of delta Q/delta t; ampere as the SI unit, with typical magnitudes (domestic appliances, lightning, nerves)

Explain currents in conductors: free electrons in metals moving against fixed positive ions, both signs of charge moving in electrolytes, no net current from random thermal motion, the momentary current from charges +Q and -Q on a cylinder, and the need for a cell to maintain a steady field
State and use Ohm's law V = RI; reason that resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area, and use R = rho l/A to find resistance or resistivity
Use current density j = I/A (A/m^2), V = El, and the forms E = rho j and j = sigma E with conductivity sigma = 1/rho
Explain the drift of electrons: acceleration eE/m, relaxation time tau, drift velocity of magnitude e E tau/m opposite to E, and use I = n e A v_d to find drift speeds and drift times

Relate conductivity to n e^2 tau/m, and answer the qualitative points of Example 3.2 (instant establishment of current, steady drift despite acceleration, large n, drift superposed on random motion, curved paths in a field)
Define mobility as drift velocity magnitude per unit field, mu = v_d/E = e tau/m, with unit m^2/V s, and compute it
State the three ways Ohm's law fails (V not proportional to I; dependence on the sign of V, as in a diode; non-unique relation, as in GaAs)
Classify conductors, semiconductors and insulators by resistivity, with metals between 10^-8 ohm m and 10^-6 ohm m

Use rho_T = rho_0 [1 + alpha (T - T0)] and the corresponding relation for resistance to find a resistance, a temperature or alpha; know its limited range of validity, that alpha is positive for metals, and the weak temperature dependence of nichrome, manganin and constantan
Explain from rho = m/(n e^2 tau) why resistivity rises with temperature in metals (tau decreases) and falls in semiconductors and insulators (n increases)
Use the energy dissipated delta W = I V delta t and power P = IV = I^2 R = V^2/R; explain where the energy comes from and why the conductor heats
Explain and calculate transmission loss Pc = I^2 Rc = P^2 Rc/V^2 and why power is transmitted at high voltage

Define emf as the open-circuit potential difference of a cell and internal resistance; use V = epsilon - I r, I = epsilon/(R + r), maximum current epsilon/r, and V = epsilon + I r for a cell being charged
Find the equivalent emf and internal resistance of cells in series (including a reversed cell) and of two cells in parallel, and use them to find currents

State Kirchhoff's junction rule and loop rule with their physical basis, and apply them, with a sign convention, to single loops and simple multi-loop networks including the symmetric cube network of Example 3.5
Describe the Wheatstone bridge, derive and use the balance condition R2/R1 = R4/R3 to find an unknown resistance, and analyse an unbalanced bridge with Kirchhoff's rules

concepts.name: Electric current and currents in conductors
concepts.description: Current as net charge crossing an area per unit time, its unit and typical magnitudes, and why a metal carries a steady current only when a steady electric field is maintained in it.
concepts.idea: Charges in motion constitute an electric current; in a solid metal the moving charges are electrons, and they give a net current only when an electric field makes their motion one-sided.
concepts.rule: For a steady current I = q/t, where q is the net charge crossing the area in the forward direction in time t (q = q+ - q-); a negative value means a current in the backward direction. For a current that is not steady, the current at time t is the limit of delta Q/delta t as delta t tends to zero. The SI unit is the ampere. With no electric field the electrons of a metal move randomly because of thermal motion, colliding with the fixed ions and emerging with the same speed in a random direction, so there is no net current. Charges +Q and -Q placed once on the ends of a metal cylinder give a current only for a very short while; a cell or battery maintains a steady field and hence a continuous current.
concepts.example: A steady current of 0.5 A carries a charge of 0.5 x 60 = 30 C across a cross-section in 1 minute.

questions.a: ampere

questions.a: at any instant as many electrons travel in any direction as in the opposite direction
o: at any instant as many electrons travel in any direction as in the opposite direction

the electrons stop moving after they collide with the fixed ions
the positive ions move so as to cancel the current of the electrons

flows steadily for as long as the discs stay attached, since the field never changes
never flows, because the electrons of a metal are bound to their atoms
starts only after the two discs have been removed

questions.q: Charges placed once at the two ends of a metal cylinder give only a momentary current, but a cell connected across it gives a continuous current. Explain the difference.
questions.a: The charges at the ends set up a field that drives electrons towards the positive end; these electrons neutralise the charges, the field disappears and the current stops after a very short while. A cell keeps supplying fresh charge to the ends to make up for the charge neutralised, so a steady electric field is maintained in the conductor and the current is continuous.
s: States that the moving electrons neutralise the end charges, so the field and the current die out
States that a cell replenishes the charges and so maintains a steady field, giving a continuous current

questions.q: A steady current of 3.2 A flows in a wire. How many electrons cross a cross-section of the wire in 1 s? Take e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C.

s: Finds the charge q = I t = 3.2 C
Divides by e to get 2 x 10^19 electrons

questions.q: In an electrolytic solution, during 4 s positive ions carrying a total charge of 6 C cross a certain area in the forward direction, while negative ions carrying a total charge of magnitude 2 C cross the same area in the backward direction. Find the net charge transported in the forward direction and the current.
questions.a: Negative charge moving backward is equivalent to positive charge moving forward, so the net charge in the forward direction is q = q+ - q- = 6 C - (-2 C) = 8 C. Current I = q/t = 8 C / 4 s = 2 A, in the forward direction.
s: Finds the net forward charge q = 6 - (-2) = 8 C
Finds I = 8/4 = 2 A in the forward direction

The current in a wire rises uniformly from 0 to 4 A in the first 5 s and then stays steady at 4 A for a further 10 s. Find (a) the charge that crosses a cross-section in the first 5 s, (b) the total charge in the whole 15 s, and (c) the steady current that would carry the same total charge in the same 15 s.
questions.a: (a) While the current rises uniformly its average value is (0 + 4)/2 = 2 A, so q1 = 2 A x 5 s = 10 C. (b) In the next 10 s, q2 = 4 A x 10 s = 40 C, so the total charge is 10 + 40 = 50 C. (c) Steady current = total charge/total time = 50 C / 15 s = 10/3 A, about 3.3 A.
s: Finds 10 C for the first 5 s using the average current 2 A
Finds 40 C for the steady part and the total 50 C
Finds the equivalent steady current 50/15 = 10/3 A (about 3.3 A)

questions.q: Assertion (A): The current I = q/t calculated across an area for a chosen forward direction can come out as a negative number. Reason (R): q is the net charge flowing across the area in the forward direction, so a negative value simply means that the current is in the backward direction.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.q: The free electrons of a metal wire move at high thermal speeds even when no battery is connected. Analyse why this fast motion produces no current, whereas the motion produced when a battery is connected does.
questions.a: Thermal motion is random: after each collision an electron's direction is completely random, so at any time as many electrons cross a given area one way as the other way and the net charge crossing is zero. When a battery maintains an electric field, the electrons are all pushed the same way (towards the positive end), so there is a net flow of charge across the area in one direction, which is a current.
s: Explains that random thermal motion gives zero net charge crossing any area
Explains that the field gives a net one-way flow of charge, i.e. a current

questions.q: Compare what happens when an electric field is applied to (a) a solid metal, (b) an electrolytic solution and (c) a material in which all the electrons remain bound to their atoms. In each case state which charges, if any, move and whether a current results.
questions.a: (a) In a solid metal the atoms are tightly bound to each other and stay fixed, but some electrons are practically free to move within the bulk, so the current is carried by negatively charged electrons moving in a background of fixed positive ions. (b) In an electrolytic solution both positive and negative charges (ions) can move, so both kinds of charge carry the current, moving in opposite directions. (c) Where the electrons remain bound they do not accelerate even when the field is applied, so no charge is transported and no current results.
s: Metal: free electrons carry the current, positive ions fixed
Electrolyte: both positive and negative charges move and carry current
Bound electrons: nothing free to move, so no current

questions.q: A student says: 'A current of 1 A in a wire is a very small current, because the nerves in our body carry far larger currents.' Evaluate this claim using the magnitudes given in the chapter.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. An ampere is typically the order of magnitude of the currents in domestic appliances, while the currents in our nerves are in microamperes, about a millionth of an ampere. So 1 A is very large compared with nerve currents; it is small only in comparison with something like lightning, which carries tens of thousands of amperes.
s: States that nerve currents are in microamperes, far smaller than 1 A, so the claim is wrong
Places 1 A correctly: typical of domestic appliances, small only beside lightning (tens of thousands of amperes)

questions.q: Construct an example of a steady current in which exactly 5 x 10^19 electrons cross a cross-section of a wire. State the current and the time you choose, show the calculation (take e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C), and state how many electrons would cross in the same time if the current were doubled.
questions.a: Charge needed: q = n e = 5 x 10^19 x 1.6 x 10^-19 C = 8 C. Any current and time with I t = 8 C will do, for example I = 2 A for t = 4 s (2 x 4 = 8 C). If the current is doubled to 4 A for the same 4 s, the charge is 16 C and the number of electrons doubles to 1 x 10^20.
s: Finds the required charge q = 8 C
Gives a current and a time whose product is 8 C, with the check shown
States that doubling the current doubles the number to 1 x 10^20

concepts.name: Ohm's law, resistance, resistivity and current density
concepts.description: Ohm's law V = RI, the dependence of resistance on length and cross-section through R = rho l/A, and the equivalent form E = rho j or j = sigma E using current density and conductivity.
concepts.idea: For a conductor obeying Ohm's law the potential difference is proportional to the current; the resistance depends on the shape of the conductor, but the resistivity depends only on the material.
concepts.rule: Ohm's law: V = R I, with R in ohm. Doubling the length of a conductor doubles its resistance and halving its cross-sectional area doubles its resistance, so R = rho l/A, where the resistivity rho depends on the material but not on its dimensions. Current per unit area taken normal to the current is the current density j = I/A, in A/m^2, directed along E. With V = E l, Ohm's law becomes E = rho j, or j = sigma E, where sigma = 1/rho is the conductivity.
concepts.example: A wire 20 m long of cross-section 4.0 x 10^-7 m^2 and resistance 2.5 ohm has resistivity rho = RA/l = 2.5 x 4.0 x 10^-7/20 = 5.0 x 10^-8 ohm m.

Uses V = E l and cancels l to obtain E = rho j

questions.q: Two wires X and Y are made from equal volumes of the same material, and X is twice as long as Y. (a) Find the ratio of their resistances R_X : R_Y. (b) If the same potential difference is applied across each, find the ratio of the currents I_X : I_Y. (c) Find the ratio of the current densities j_X : j_Y.
questions.a: (a) Equal volumes: A_X l_X = A_Y l_Y, so with l_X = 2 l_Y we get A_X = A_Y/2. R = rho l/A gives R_X/R_Y = (2)/(1/2) = 4, so R_X : R_Y = 4 : 1. (b) For the same V, I = V/R, so I_X : I_Y = 1 : 4. (c) j = I/A, so j_X/j_Y = (1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2, i.e. j_X : j_Y = 1 : 2. (Check: j = sigma E with E = V/l, and X is twice as long.)

questions.a: It is wrong. Resistivity is a property of the material and does not depend on the dimensions of the conductor, so both copper wires have the same resistivity. What is lower for the thick wire is its resistance, because R = rho l/A and its cross-sectional area A is larger.
s: States that resistivity depends on the material, not the dimensions, so it is the same for both wires
Explains that it is the resistance R = rho l/A that is lower for the thick wire

questions.q: Design a wire of resistance 10 ohm from a material of resistivity 5 x 10^-7 ohm m. Choose a length and a cross-sectional area, show that the resistance is 10 ohm, and find the current density in your wire when a potential difference of 5 V is applied across it.
questions.a: R = rho l/A = 10 ohm needs l/A = 10/(5 x 10^-7) = 2 x 10^7 per metre. For example choose A = 1 x 10^-6 m^2 and l = 20 m: R = (5 x 10^-7 x 20)/(1 x 10^-6) = 10 ohm. With 5 V applied, I = V/R = 0.5 A, so j = I/A = 0.5/(1 x 10^-6) = 5 x 10^5 A/m^2. (Other choices with l/A = 2 x 10^7 per metre are equally valid; j then equals 0.5 A divided by the chosen area.)
s: Chooses l and A with l/A = 2 x 10^7 per metre
Verifies R = rho l/A = 10 ohm
Finds I = 0.5 A and the current density for the chosen area

concepts.name: Drift of electrons, relaxation time and mobility
concepts.description: The drift velocity of electrons in a field, the relation I = n e A v_d, the conductivity in terms of relaxation time, and mobility.
concepts.idea: An electric field gives the randomly moving electrons of a metal a small steady average velocity, the drift velocity, and this drift of an enormous number of electrons is the current.
concepts.rule: Between collisions an electron has acceleration of magnitude eE/m. Averaging over the electrons, with tau the average time between collisions (relaxation time), the drift velocity has magnitude v_d = e E tau/m and is directed opposite to E; it is independent of time. The current is I = n e A v_d, where n is the number of free electrons per unit volume, so j = (n e^2 tau/m) E, which is Ohm's law with conductivity sigma = n e^2 tau/m. Mobility is the magnitude of the drift velocity per unit electric field, mu = v_d/E = e tau/m, in m^2/V s. The drift speed is tiny (about a millimetre per second for a few amperes in a copper wire), far smaller than thermal speeds or the speed at which the field is established.

questions.q: The average time between successive collisions of an electron with the ions of a metal is called the ____ time (one word).
questions.a: relaxation

o: the magnitude of its drift velocity per unit electric field

questions.a: All the free electrons of the metal move in the same direction
o: All the free electrons of the metal move in the same direction
The drift velocity is superposed on the much larger random velocities of the electrons
For a steady field, the average drift velocity is independent of time
The drift speed is far smaller than the speed at which the electric field is established along the conductor

questions.q: The drift velocity of the electrons in a conductor is directed
questions.a: opposite to the electric field

The drift speed of electrons is only about a millimetre per second, yet a current is established almost the instant a circuit is closed. This is because
questions.a: the electric field is set up throughout the circuit almost instantly, causing a local electron drift at every point
o: the electric field is set up throughout the circuit almost instantly, causing a local electron drift at every point
the electrons near the battery travel to the far end of the circuit at the speed of light
the electrons were already drifting along the wire before the circuit was closed

questions.a: an electron loses its drift speed in each collision with an ion and has to start accelerating again

the electric field inside a current-carrying conductor is zero
the electrons are too heavy to be accelerated by the field
the force of the field is exactly balanced by the weight of the electron

questions.a: The current is I = n e A v_d. Although e and v_d are small, the number density n of free electrons in a metal is enormous, of the order of 10^29 per m^3, so the product n e A v_d can be a large current.
s: Writes I = n e A v_d
States that the electron number density is enormous (about 10^29 per m^3), which makes the current large

questions.q: Electrons in a wire have a drift speed of 2 x 10^-4 m/s when the electric field in the wire is 0.5 V/m. Their mobility is

concepts.name: Limitations of Ohm's law and temperature dependence of resistivity
concepts.description: The ways in which materials and devices deviate from Ohm's law, the resistivity ranges of metals, semiconductors and insulators, and how resistivity changes with temperature.
concepts.idea: Ohm's law is not a fundamental law, and resistivity is not a fixed number: it differs enormously between materials and changes with temperature, rising for metals and falling for semiconductors.
concepts.rule: Ohm's law fails when V ceases to be proportional to I, when the relation between V and I depends on the sign of V (as in a diode), or when the relation is not unique (as in GaAs). Metals have resistivities from 10^-8 ohm m to 10^-6 ohm m; insulators are higher by an enormous factor; semiconductors lie in between. Over a limited range of temperature the resistivity of a metal is rho_T = rho_0 [1 + alpha (T - T0)], with the temperature coefficient of resistivity alpha positive for metals; for a wire the same relation holds for resistance, R2 = R1 [1 + alpha (T2 - T1)]. Since rho = m/(n e^2 tau), heating a metal shortens tau and raises rho, while in semiconductors and insulators n increases with temperature and rho falls. Nichrome, manganin and constantan depend only weakly on temperature.
concepts.example: A wire of resistance 10 ohm at 20 degrees C with alpha = 4 x 10^-3 per degree C has resistance 10 [1 + 4 x 10^-3 x 50] = 12 ohm at 70 degrees C.

concepts.name: Electrical energy and power
concepts.description: Energy dissipated as heat in a conductor, the power expressions P = IV = I^2 R = V^2/R, and why power is transmitted at high voltage.
concepts.idea: Charge moving through a conductor loses potential energy; because of collisions this energy appears as heat in the conductor, at a rate equal to the current times the potential difference.
concepts.rule: When a current I flows through a conductor across which the potential difference is V, the energy dissipated as heat in time delta t is delta W = I V delta t, so the power is P = I V. Using V = IR, P = I^2 R = V^2/R (the ohmic loss). The power comes from the source, for a cell from its chemical energy. To deliver a power P at voltage V through cables of resistance Rc, the current is I = P/V and the power wasted in the cables is Pc = I^2 Rc = P^2 Rc/V^2, inversely proportional to V^2, which is why power is transmitted at very high voltage and lowered by a transformer at the other end.
concepts.example: A device taking 10 kW at 200 V draws 50 A, wasting 50^2 x 1 = 2500 W in cables of 1 ohm; at 2000 V it draws 5 A and wastes only 25 W.

concepts.description: The emf of a cell as its open-circuit potential difference, its internal resistance, the terminal potential difference V = epsilon - I r and the current I = epsilon/(R + r).
concepts.idea: A cell maintains a steady current; its emf is the potential difference between its electrodes when no current flows, and when it delivers current part of this is lost across the internal resistance of its electrolyte.
concepts.rule: The emf epsilon of a cell is the potential difference between its positive and negative electrodes in an open circuit; it is a potential difference, not a force. The electrolyte has a finite internal resistance r. When the cell sends a current I through an external resistance R, the potential difference between its terminals is V = epsilon - I r, and since V = I R, the current is I = epsilon/(R + r). The maximum current, for R = 0, is epsilon/r. If the current is driven through the cell from its positive to its negative terminal (as in charging), V = epsilon + I r.
concepts.example: A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 1 ohm connected to a 4 ohm resistor gives I = 2/(4 + 1) = 0.4 A and a terminal potential difference of 2 - 0.4 x 1 = 1.6 V.

(b) During charging the current enters the battery at its positive terminal, so V = epsilon + I r = 12 + 4 x 1 = 16 V. (c) The series resistor limits the charging current. Without it the current would be (100 - 12)/1 = 88 A, which is dangerously large and would damage the battery.

Finds the terminal voltage 12 + 4 x 1 = 16 V

questions.q: A cell sends a current of 1.0 A through a 2 ohm resistor and, when that resistor is replaced, a current of 0.5 A through a 5 ohm resistor. Find the emf and the internal resistance of the cell.
questions.a: epsilon = I (R + r) in both cases: epsilon = 1.0 (2 + r) and epsilon = 0.5 (5 + r). So 2 + r = 2.5 + 0.5 r, giving 0.5 r = 0.5 and r = 1 ohm. Then epsilon = 1.0 x (2 + 1) = 3 V.

Finds epsilon = 3 V

questions.q: A cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 ohm is connected in turn to external resistors of 1 ohm, 2 ohm and 5 ohm. questions.a: I = epsilon/(R + r) and V = epsilon - I r. For 1 ohm: I = 6/2 = 3 A, V = 6 - 3 = 3 V. For 2 ohm: I = 6/3 = 2 A, V = 6 - 2 = 4 V. For 5 ohm: I = 6/6 = 1 A, V = 6 - 1 = 5 V. As R increases the current falls, the drop I r across the internal resistance falls, and the terminal potential difference rises towards the emf of 6 V (reaching it only on open circuit).
s: Finds the three currents 3 A, 2 A and 1 A
Finds the three terminal potential differences 3 V, 4 V and 5 V
States that V approaches the emf as R increases because I r becomes smaller

questions.q: A cell is marked 1.5 V. A student measures 1.4 V across its terminals while it is lighting a bulb and concludes that the marking must be wrong. Evaluate this conclusion.
questions.a: The conclusion is not justified. The marked value is the emf, the potential difference between the terminals on open circuit. When the cell delivers a current I, the terminal potential difference is V = epsilon - I r, which is less than the emf by the drop I r across the internal resistance. A reading of 1.4 V under load is consistent with an emf of 1.5 V.
s: States that the emf is the open-circuit potential difference
Uses V = epsilon - I r to explain the lower reading while current flows

questions.q: Design a circuit of one cell and one external resistor in which the terminal potential difference of the cell is exactly 90% of its emf. Choose the emf, the internal resistance and the external resistance, and show the current and the terminal potential difference.

Chooses values satisfying it and finds the current
Shows the terminal potential difference is 90% of the emf

concepts.name: Cells in series and in parallel
concepts.description: Replacing a series or a parallel combination of cells by a single equivalent cell, with its equivalent emf and equivalent internal resistance.
concepts.idea: Like resistors, cells can be combined, and for calculating currents and voltages a combination of cells can be replaced by one equivalent cell.
concepts.rule: Series (current leaving each cell from its positive electrode): epsilon_eq = epsilon1 + epsilon2 and r_eq = r1 + r2; a cell from which the current leaves at the negative electrode enters with a negative sign, so with the two negatives joined epsilon_eq = epsilon1 - epsilon2 (epsilon1 > epsilon2), while the internal resistances still add. Parallel (positive terminals joined together and negative terminals joined together): I = I1 + I2, epsilon_eq = (epsilon1 r2 + epsilon2 r1)/(r1 + r2) and r_eq = r1 r2/(r1 + r2), equivalently 1/r_eq = 1/r1 + 1/r2 and epsilon_eq/r_eq = epsilon1/r1 + epsilon2/r2. Both rules extend to n cells.
concepts.example: Cells of 6 V, 2 ohm and 3 V, 1 ohm in parallel give epsilon_eq = (6 x 1 + 3 x 2)/(2 + 1) = 4 V and r_eq = (2 x 1)/(2 + 1) = 2/3 ohm.

questions.q: When cells are connected in series so that the current leaves each cell from its positive electrode, the equivalent emf is the ____ of their individual emfs (one word).

Across the combination V_AC = V_AB + V_BC = (epsilon1 + epsilon2) - I (r1 + r2). Comparing with V = epsilon_eq - I r_eq for a single cell gives epsilon_eq = epsilon1 + epsilon2 and r_eq = r1 + r2.

Compares with epsilon_eq - I r_eq to identify the equivalent emf and internal resistance

Finds I = 0.5 A and the potential difference 5 V

(c) For each cell V = epsilon - I r, so I1 = (12 - 6)/2 = 3 A and I2 = (6 - 6)/2 = 0 A. The 6 V cell delivers no current, and I1 + I2 = 3 A as required.

Finds I = 3 A and V = 6 V

questions.a: The reversed cell enters with a negative sign: epsilon_eq = 2 + 2 - 2 = 2 V. Internal resistances still add: r_eq = 3 x 0.5 = 1.5 ohm. I = epsilon_eq/(R + r_eq) = 2/(2.5 + 1.5) = 0.5 A.

questions.a: Series: epsilon_eq = 6 V, r_eq = 4 ohm. Parallel: epsilon_eq = 3 V, r_eq = 1 ohm. (a) For 8 ohm: series I = 6/(8 + 4) = 0.5 A; parallel I = 3/(8 + 1) = 1/3 A, about 0.33 A. (b) For 1 ohm: series I = 6/(1 + 4) = 1.2 A; parallel I = 3/(1 + 1) = 1.5 A. (c) Series gives the larger current through the large external resistance, where the doubled emf matters more than the added internal resistance; parallel gives the larger current through the small external resistance, where the reduced internal resistance matters more.

Finds 0.5 A and 1/3 A for 8 ohm, and 1.2 A and 1.5 A for 1 ohm

questions.q: A student connects a 2 V cell and a 4 V cell of equal internal resistance in parallel, like terminals joined, and claims the combination is equivalent to a 6 V cell. Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong; emfs add only in a series combination. In parallel, epsilon_eq = (epsilon1 r2 + epsilon2 r1)/(r1 + r2). With r1 = r2 = r this is (2 r + 4 r)/(2 r) = 3 V, so the combination is equivalent to a 3 V cell (with internal resistance r/2).
s: States that adding emfs applies to series, not parallel, combinations
Uses the parallel formula with equal internal resistances to get 3 V

questions.q: Design a parallel combination (like terminals joined) of two cells with different emfs and different internal resistances whose equivalent emf is exactly 5 V. State your values, verify the equivalent emf and find the equivalent internal resistance.
questions.a: We need (epsilon1 r2 + epsilon2 r1)/(r1 + r2) = 5 V. For example epsilon1 = 6 V, r1 = 1 ohm and epsilon2 = 3 V, r2 = 2 ohm: epsilon_eq = (6 x 2 + 3 x 1)/(1 + 2) = 15/3 = 5 V. r_eq = r1 r2/(r1 + r2) = (1 x 2)/(1 + 2) = 2/3 ohm.
s: States two different emfs and two different internal resistances
Verifies epsilon_eq = 5 V with the parallel formula
Finds r_eq for the chosen values

concepts.name: Kirchhoff's rules
concepts.description: The junction rule and the loop rule, their physical basis, and their use to find the currents in a network of resistors and cells.
concepts.idea: Any network of cells and resistors can be analysed with two rules: charge does not pile up at a junction, and the potential returns to its starting value around a closed loop.
concepts.rule: Label a current with a symbol and an arrow in each branch; a negative result means the actual current is opposite to the arrow. Junction rule: at any junction the sum of the currents entering equals the sum of the currents leaving (for steady currents charge does not accumulate at any point). Loop rule: the algebraic sum of the changes in potential around any closed loop involving resistors and cells is zero (potential depends only on location). Going through a resistor R along the current I the change is -IR; going through a cell from its negative to its positive terminal the change is +epsilon. Use as many junctions and loops as are needed to solve for the unknowns.
concepts.example: A loop with a 12 V cell and resistors of 2 ohm and 4 ohm: 12 - 2 I - 4 I = 0, so I = 2 A.

questions.q: State the physical reason behind (a) Kirchhoff's junction rule and (b) Kirchhoff's loop rule.
questions.a: (a) When currents are steady there is no accumulation of charge at any junction or at any point in a line, so the rate at which charge flows into a junction must equal the rate at which it flows out. (b) Electric potential depends only on the location of the point, so on starting from any point and coming back to the same point round a closed loop the total change in potential must be zero.
s: Junction rule: no accumulation of charge at a junction for steady currents
Loop rule: potential depends only on position, so the total change round a closed loop is zero

questions.q: A single closed loop contains a cell of emf 12 V with negligible internal resistance and two resistors of 2 ohm and 4 ohm, all connected one after another. Applying the loop rule, the current in the loop is

questions.q: Five wires meet at a junction. Currents of 4 A and 3 A enter the junction through two of them, and currents of 2 A and 1 A leave through two others. The current in the fifth wire is

questions.q: A single closed loop contains a cell of emf 10 V and a cell of emf 4 V, each of internal resistance 1 ohm, connected so that their emfs oppose each other, and a 4 ohm resistor. Use the loop rule to find the current and the potential difference across the 4 ohm resistor.
questions.a: Going round the loop in the direction of the current I (driven by the 10 V cell): +10 - 4 - I (1) - I (1) - I (4) = 0, so 6 I = 6 and I = 1 A. Potential difference across the 4 ohm resistor = I R = 1 x 4 = 4 V.
s: Writes the loop equation 10 - 4 - 6 I = 0 and finds I = 1 A
Finds the potential difference 4 V across the 4 ohm resistor

questions.q: A cell of emf 9 V and negligible internal resistance is connected across two points P and Q. A 3 ohm resistor and a 6 ohm resistor are each connected directly between P and Q. Use the loop rule for the loop containing the cell and each resistor in turn to find the current in each resistor, and the junction rule to find the current through the cell.
questions.a: Loop through the cell and the 3 ohm resistor: 9 - 3 I1 = 0, so I1 = 3 A. Loop through the cell and the 6 ohm resistor: 9 - 6 I2 = 0, so I2 = 1.5 A. Junction rule at P: current through the cell I = I1 + I2 = 3 + 1.5 = 4.5 A.
s: Uses the loop rule to find I1 = 3 A and I2 = 1.5 A
Uses the junction rule to find the cell current 4.5 A

questions.q: Points a and b are joined by three branches. Branch 1 has a cell of emf 14 V, its positive terminal towards a, in series with a 2 ohm resistor. Branch 2 has a cell of emf 10 V, its positive terminal towards a, in series with a 2 ohm resistor. Branch 3 is a 2 ohm resistor alone. Internal resistances are negligible. Using Kirchhoff's rules, find the current in each branch.
questions.a: Let I1 and I2 flow through branches 1 and 2 towards a, and I3 flow from a to b through branch 3. Junction rule at a: I3 = I1 + I2. Loop through branch 1 and branch 3: 14 - 2 I1 - 2 I3 = 0. Loop through branch 2 and branch 3: 10 - 2 I2 - 2 I3 = 0. Adding the loop equations: 24 - 2 (I1 + I2) - 4 I3 = 0, so 24 = 6 I3 and I3 = 4 A. Then I1 = (14 - 8)/2 = 3 A and I2 = (10 - 8)/2 = 1 A. So branch 1 carries 3 A and branch 2 carries 1 A, both towards a, and branch 3 carries 4 A from a to b.
s: Writes the junction equation I3 = I1 + I2
Writes the two loop equations 14 - 2 I1 - 2 I3 = 0 and 10 - 2 I2 - 2 I3 = 0
Solves to get I1 = 3 A, I2 = 1 A, I3 = 4 A

Using symmetry and the junction rule, find the current in each of the three edges meeting at the entry corner, and in each of the edges into which those currents next divide.
questions.a: The three edges meeting at the entry corner are symmetrically placed, so the current 3I divides equally among them: each carries I. At the far end of each of these edges the incoming current I must split equally into the two outgoing edges, so each of those six edges carries I/2.
s: Uses symmetry and the junction rule at the entry corner to get I in each of the three edges
Uses the junction rule at the next corners to get I/2 in each of the six following edges

questions.q: Twelve resistors, each of 6 ohm, form the edges of a cube. A battery of emf 10 V and negligible internal resistance is connected across two diagonally opposite corners. Using symmetry and Kirchhoff's rules, find the equivalent resistance of the network, the total current drawn from the battery and the currents in the edges.
questions.a: Let the total current be 3I. By symmetry each of the three edges at the entry corner carries I, each of the six middle edges carries I/2, and each of the three edges meeting at the exit corner carries I. Loop rule for a closed loop through the battery and one path across the cube (three edges): -I R - (1/2) I R - I R + epsilon = 0, so epsilon = (5/2) I R. Equivalent resistance R_eq = epsilon/(3I) = (5/6) R = (5/6) x 6 = 5 ohm. Total current = 10 V / 5 ohm = 2 A, so I = 2/3 A: the six edges at the entry and exit corners carry 2/3 A each and the six middle edges carry 1/3 A each.
s: Assigns currents I, I/2, I to the three kinds of edge using symmetry and the junction rule
Applies the loop rule to get epsilon = (5/2) I R and R_eq = (5/6) R = 5 ohm
Finds the total current 2 A and the edge currents 2/3 A and 1/3 A

questions.q: For a network with three unknown currents, a student writes the loop rule for four different closed loops and expects to obtain four independent equations. Evaluate this expectation.
questions.a: The expectation is wrong. Three unknown currents need only three independent equations. States that further loops give no new independent equation and are automatically satisfied

questions.q: Design a single closed loop containing two cells of different emfs connected so that they oppose each other, and two resistors, in which the current is exactly 0.5 A. questions.a: For example, cells of 12 V and 6 V opposing each other, with resistors of 4 ohm and 8 ohm. Going round in the direction of the current (driven by the 12 V cell): +12 - 6 - 4 I - 8 I = 0, so 12 I = 6 and I = 0.5 A. Potential differences: 0.5 x 4 = 2 V and 0.5 x 8 = 4 V, which together equal the net emf of 6 V.
s: Chooses two opposing emfs and two resistors with (difference of emfs)/(total resistance) = 0.5 A
Writes the loop equation and shows I = 0.5 A
Finds the potential difference across each resistor

concepts.name: Wheatstone bridge
concepts.description: The four-resistor bridge circuit, its balance condition obtained from Kirchhoff's rules, and its use to find an unknown resistance.
concepts.idea: Four resistors form a bridge; when their values are in the right proportion no current flows through the galvanometer, and this null condition lets one resistance be found from the other three.
concepts.rule: Four resistors form the arms of a bridge ABCD: R1 in arm AD, R2 in arm AB, R3 in arm DC and R4 in arm BC. A source is connected across A and C (the battery arm) and a galvanometer across B and D (the galvanometer arm). In a balanced bridge the galvanometer current is zero; the junction rule then gives I1 = I3 and I2 = I4, and the loop rule for loops ADBA and CBDC gives the balance condition R2/R1 = R4/R3, i.e. R_AB/R_AD = R_BC/R_DC. With known R1 and R2, R3 is varied until the galvanometer shows null deflection, and the unknown is R4 = R3 R2/R1. An unbalanced bridge is solved with Kirchhoff's rules.
concepts.example: With AB = 10 ohm, BC = 20 ohm and AD = 30 ohm, the bridge balances when DC = 30 x 20/10 = 60 ohm.

questions.q: A Wheatstone bridge ABCD (source connected across A and C, galvanometer connected across B and D) has arms AB = 6 ohm, BC = 3 ohm, AD = 4 ohm and DC = 2 ohm. The source has emf 9 V and negligible internal resistance. Show that the bridge is balanced and find the current drawn from the source.

The same current then flows through AB and BC: loop rule gives 9 - I (6 + 3) = 0, so I = 1 A. Similarly for AD and DC: 9 - I' (4 + 2) = 0, so I' = 1.5 A. Junction rule at A: current from the source = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 A.

questions.q: A bridge network ABCD has arms AB = 4 ohm, BC = 2 ohm, AD = 2 ohm and DC = 4 ohm, and a 4 ohm resistor connected between B and D. A source of emf 10 V and negligible internal resistance is connected across A and C, with A at the higher potential. Using Kirchhoff's rules, find the current in each of the five resistors and the current drawn from the source.

Loop through AB, BC and the source: 10 - 4 I1 - 2 (I1 + Ig) = 0. Loop through AD, DC and the source: 10 - 2 I2 - 4 (I2 - Ig) = 0. Solving: I1 = 1.5 A, I2 = 2 A, Ig = 0.5 A. So AB carries 1.5 A, BC carries 2 A, AD carries 2 A, DC carries 1.5 A and the resistor BD carries 0.5 A from D to B. Current from the source = I1 + I2 = 3.5 A.

(c) With DC = 30 ohm and the galvanometer disconnected, the potential of B above C is 18 x 40/60 = 12 V and that of D above C is 18 x 30/60 = 9 V. B is at the higher potential, so current flows through the galvanometer from B to D.

Finds 0.3 A in AB and BC, 0.2 A in AD and DC, and 0.5 A from the source
Finds 12 V at B and 9 V at D, so the galvanometer current is from B to D
